hints: Notice the wording $\beta^+$ particle, which is a positron emitted when a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron.
Recall that $\beta$ decay must conserve charge, nucleon number, energy and lepton number, so a second very light lepton must carry away energy.
Compare the two $\beta$ decays: $\beta^-$ decay involves an antineutrino, so check what lepton-number conservation requires when the emitted charged lepton is antimatter.
walkthrough: Identify the $\beta^+$ decay process inside the nucleus: a proton changes into a neutron, $p \rightarrow n + \beta^+ + \text{other particle}$.
Check conservation: nucleon number is conserved ($1 \rightarrow 1 + 0 + 0$) and charge is conserved ($+1 \rightarrow 0 + 1 + 0$), so the other particle must have zero charge and zero nucleon number.
Apply lepton number conservation. The $\beta^+$ particle is a positron, which is antimatter with lepton number $-1$, while the initial proton has lepton number $0$.
To keep total lepton number at $0$, the other emitted particle must have lepton number $+1$ and almost no mass, which is the property of a neutrino.
The full equation is $p \rightarrow n + {}_{+1}^{0}\beta + \nu_e$, where $\nu_e$ is the electron neutrino. This is option D.

options.A: An antineutrino is emitted with a $\beta^-$ particle, not with a $\beta^+$ particle, as it is needed to balance lepton number for neutron decay.
options.B: A $\beta^-$ particle is an electron emitted in a separate decay when a neutron changes to a proton, and it cannot be emitted together with a $\beta^+$ particle.
options.C: An $\alpha$-particle is a helium nucleus emitted in alpha decay and is unrelated to the proton to neutron change in $\beta^+$ decay.
options.D: In $\beta^+$ decay a proton changes to a neutron, and a neutrino is emitted with the positron to conserve energy and lepton number.
